warmup.q: A C program takes and releases a lock one million times on one thread, and no other thread ever wants that lock. A system call is a request from a program to the kernel. About how many system calls does that loop make?
options: About 1,000,000: every lock asks the kernel
About 2,000,000: one to take the lock and one to release it
warmup.why: Taking a lock nobody else holds is one compare-and-swap on a number in the program's own memory, and releasing it is one more atomic instruction; the first section explains both. The kernel is called only when a thread has to sleep or wake someone. In the lab box, a million pairs made exactly one futex call, and that one came from pthread_join, the main thread waiting for the worker to finish. The first two options are tempting, because only the kernel can make a thread wait. The trick is to ask it only when someone really has to.

sections.h: Two threads, one balance: a lock needs an instruction that can't be split
sections.html:
Let's start with the smallest program that goes wrong. Two threads of the payments program add to the same shop balance at once. Each runs balance = balance + 50. That looks like one step, but the CPU does it in three: load the value from memory into a register (one of its small working slots), add 50, and store the result back. If both threads load 100 before either stores, both store 150. Two payments came in, and one of them is gone.

Shared data needs a lock: a promise that only one thread at a time runs the code between lock() and unlock(). That stretch of code is the critical section. The café's one bathroom works the same way. One person goes in and locks the door, and everyone else waits outside.

The simplest lock is a flag: if (!locked) { locked = true; ... }. It fails for the same reason the balance did. Checking the flag and setting it are two steps, and the scheduler (the part of the kernel that decides which thread runs) can switch threads between them. Here are two threads, T1 and T2:

T1: reads locked = false
T2: reads locked = false
T1: locked = true, enters the critical section
T2: locked = true, enters the critical section     both inside

Both threads are inside. It's two people who both read Vacant on the bathroom door, and both walked in.

The fix comes from the hardware. CPUs have atomic instructions, which read and write a word of memory (here, 4 bytes) in one step that no other CPU can split. The one locks are built on is compare-and-swap (CAS): "if this word holds 0, put 1 in it, and tell me whether you did". If two threads race to CAS the same word, exactly one wins. On arm64, the chip design in Apple Silicon Macs, it's the CAS family of instructions (older chips use a pair of special load and store instructions). On x86, the design in Intel and AMD chips, it's LOCK CMPXCHG. Java offers it as AtomicInteger.compareAndSet.

A lock that loops on CAS until it wins is a spinlock. The kernel uses spinlocks inside itself, for critical sections that last nanoseconds (billionths of a second). In ordinary programs, a spinlock goes wrong when the thread holding it isn't running. CPU scheduling: EEVDF, nice and CPU quotas showed that the scheduler can take the CPU away from a thread in the middle of its work. If that thread holds the lock, every waiter spins through its whole 3 ms turn on a lock that can't be released until the holder runs again.

So a waiter should sleep, and only the kernel can put a thread to sleep and wake it later. The naive design asks the kernel every time a thread takes or releases the lock. A system call, a request from a program to the kernel, costs about 150 ns, as the first lesson of this track measured. Taking and releasing a lock nobody else wants costs a few nanoseconds inside the program: one million pairs on one thread take 8 ms in the Try it below. Two system calls per pair would make that common case nearly 40 times slower.

We want both: no kernel when nobody waits, and real sleep when someone does. Next, we'll see how Linux gets both from one word of memory.

try.title: Time a lock with and without contention
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. os/c/l05/counter.c starts N threads that each add 1 to a shared balance a million times, under one pthread mutex, the standard lock of C programs on Linux. time reports how long a command took: real on the clock, user in the program's own code and sys in the kernel.
Predict how long one million lock() and unlock() pairs take on one thread. Then predict four threads: four times as long, or worse?

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -pthread -o /tmp/counter os/c/l05/counter.c time /tmp/counter 1 time /tmp/counter 4

try.expect:
Timings vary a little between runs:

1 threads: balance = 1000000 (expected 1000000)

real	0m0.008s
user	0m0.007s
sys	0m0.001s
4 threads: balance = 4000000 (expected 4000000)

real	0m0.174s
user	0m0.257s
sys	0m0.292s

One thread: about 8 ns to take and release the lock, all inside the program (sys is 1 ms). Four threads did four times the work and took over 20 times as long, and more of their CPU time went to the kernel (sys) than to the program's own code (user). The balance is right both times, so the lock works. Contention, threads wanting the same lock at once, is what costs.

sections.h: A futex keeps the kernel out until someone has to wait
sections.html:
Back to the café's bathroom. Most visits need nobody's help. You see Vacant, you go in and lock the door, and later you unlock it. Only when the door is already locked do you go to the counter and ask the barista to call you when it's free. And whoever comes out only goes to the counter if someone is waiting.

A futex (fast user-space mutex) works the same way. A mutex is another name for a lock, and user space is where ordinary programs run, outside the kernel. The lock itself is a 32-bit number in the program's own memory, called the futex word, and taking or releasing it is a CAS on that word. The kernel joins in only when a thread has to wait, through one system call, futex, with two operations that matter here:

  • FUTEX_WAIT(addr, expected): put me to sleep, but only if the word at address addr still holds expected. The kernel reads the word, compares it and starts the sleep as one atomic step. If the word has changed, the call fails at once with EAGAIN, an error code that means "try again".
  • FUTEX_WAKE(addr, n): wake up to n threads sleeping on addr.

The kernel keeps a wait queue, a list of sleeping threads, for each address, and nothing at all for a futex nobody is waiting on.

glibc, the C library that almost every Linux program is built on, gives the word three values in its mutex: 0 is free, 1 is locked, and 2 is locked with someone waiting. Ulrich Drepper's paper "Futexes Are Tricky" walks through why it takes three. To lock, CAS the word from 0 to 1. If that works, you're done, with no system call. If not, set the word to 2 and call FUTEX_WAIT(addr, 2). To release, swap the word to 0, and only if the old value was 2, call FUTEX_WAKE(addr, 1). The 2 is a note on the bathroom door that says someone is waiting.

The check inside FUTEX_WAIT prevents a lost wake-up. Without it, T2 could decide to sleep, and T1 could release the lock and wake nobody, because T2 isn't asleep yet. Then T2 would sleep forever on a free lock. The check is the barista glancing at the door once more before writing your name down. If the word is no longer 2, the kernel sends T2 back to try again.

The picture breaks at fairness. A barista calls people in order. A woken thread has to race any newcomer for the CAS, and the newcomer, already running, often wins.

You can watch both paths. strace is a tool that prints or counts every system call a program makes. Under strace -c, one thread taking a pthread mutex a million times makes 1 futex call, and that one is pthread_join, the main thread waiting for the worker to end. Four threads make 2,749, and 1,042 of them fail with EAGAIN: the race in the last frame of the stepper, over and over.

The JVM, the program that runs Java code, sits on the same mechanism. ReentrantLock, one of Java's lock classes, takes the lock with a CAS on a number inside the lock object. When it has to wait, it parks the thread (puts it to sleep) with LockSupport.park, which on Linux ends in a futex wait. synchronized, Java's built-in lock, also starts with a CAS inside the program and sleeps through the kernel only when another thread holds the lock. So "is this lock slow?" really asks "how often do threads find it taken?".

Making waiting cheap has a side effect: a thread that waits forever costs nothing either. Next, we'll make two threads do exactly that.

In one step, the kernel checks that the word still holds 2 and puts T2 on the wait queue for that address. ps, the command that lists processes and threads, would now show T2 asleep in futex_wait_queue, using no CPU. That's the first system call.

frames.say: The kernel moves T2 off the wait queue, and the scheduler runs it. T2 swaps the word to 2 and sees the old value 0: it owns the lock. It sets 2, not 1, because it can't know whether other threads are still asleep. So when it releases the lock, it will make one wake call that may not be needed. That's the price of keeping the kernel out of the fast path.

The kernel compares, finds 0 instead of the expected 2, and returns EAGAIN at once instead of sleeping. T2 tries again. Without that check, T2 could sleep forever on a lock nobody holds. These are the errors in the futex row of the strace counts.

video.title: A futex: the lock that asks the kernel only when someone waits

sections.h: A deadlock: two transfers, each holding the lock the other needs
sections.html:
Futexes make waiting cheap. They also make a mistake quiet. Back to the opening. A refund moves 120 (amounts are in cents, so that's 1.20) from the shop's account to the customer's. At the same moment, a payment for a smaller coffee moves 80 the other way. Each transfer locks its source account, then its target, so that both balances change while it holds both locks:

synchronized (from) {
    synchronized (to) {
        from.balance -= amount;
        to.balance += amount;
    }
}

synchronized (from) means "take the lock that belongs to the object from, and release it at the closing brace".

Run them together, and the refund can lock the shop's account while the payment locks the customer's. Now the refund waits for the customer's account, which the payment holds. The payment waits for the shop's, which the refund holds. Neither can go on, and neither will let go of what it has. That's a deadlock. In the café, it's two staff at closing time: one holds the till key and waits for the safe key, and the other holds the safe key and waits for the till key. Try to cause one in the simulator below.

Four conditions must all hold for a deadlock. OSTEP, a free operating-systems textbook, lists them after Edward Coffman and colleagues, who set them out in 1971:

  1. Mutual exclusion: a lock has one owner at a time.
  2. Hold and wait: a thread keeps the locks it has while it waits for another.
  3. No preemption: nothing can take a lock away from the thread that holds it.
  4. Circular wait: there's a loop of threads, each waiting for a lock that the next one holds.

The last condition is the one you can draw. Put an arrow from each waiting thread to the thread that holds the lock it wants. That's a wait-for graph, and a deadlock is a loop in it. Here the graph is refund to payment, and payment back to refund. jstack, a tool that comes with Java and prints every thread of a running JVM, builds the same graph from the JVM's records of who holds which lock. It prints the loop as "Found one Java-level deadlock".

The kernel sees none of it. To the kernel, both threads are asleep in futex_wait_queue, using no CPU, exactly like idle threads waiting for work. Nothing times out, and the JVM doesn't break the loop either. The two threads, and every later payment that needs either account, stay stuck until the program restarts. That's the opening's card reader: a program with idle CPUs whose answers never come back.

A deadlock needs all four conditions at once. Next, we'll use that: a fix only has to remove one.

sim.title: A refund and a payment lock the same two accounts
sim.intro: You're the scheduler: pick which transfer runs its next line. The locks are the two accounts: `ACC-1001` is the shop's (called `merchant` in the code) and `ACC-2002` is the customer's. First make the transfers deadlock. Then reset, and get both to finish with the shop's balance at 9960.

goal.say: Both transfers finished: 10,000 - 120 + 80 = 9,960. Every order that works lets one transfer take both locks before the other takes its first. Run line 1 of the refund and line 1 of the payment back to back, and nothing can finish.

steps: Transfers naive runs this section's refund and payment at the same time. A 50 ms pause between taking the two locks makes the deadlock happen on every run.
Look from the kernel's side with ps (-L gives one line per thread, and the WCHAN column names the kernel function a thread sleeps in), then from the JVM's side with jstack.

Thread ids and addresses differ between runs:

pid 40: naive locks
still waiting after 3 s: deadlock
  TID %CPU STAT WCHAN                COMMAND
   62  0.0 Sl   futex_wait_queue     refund
   63  0.0 Sl   futex_wait_queue     payment
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"refund":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x0000ffff280021a0 (object 0x000000008bb19370, a sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers$Account),
  which is held by "payment"

"payment":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x0000ffff20000ed0 (object 0x000000008bb191f8, a sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers$Account),
  which is held by "refund"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:

The kernel's view: two sleeping threads (S in the STAT column) at 0.0% CPU, parked in futex_wait_queue, the kernel side of FUTEX_WAIT. Nothing about them looks wrong. The JVM's view: a loop of two, refund waiting for payment and payment waiting for refund.

sections.h: Remove one of the four conditions, and the deadlock can't happen
sections.html:
All four conditions are needed, so a fix only has to remove one. Each fix below removes a different one, and each has a price.

Remove circular wait with a lock order. Pick one order for all the locks, say by account number, and always lock the smaller number first, whichever way the money goes. Both transfers now start with ACC-1001. Whoever gets it also gets the second lock. The other waits for its first lock while holding nothing, so no loop can form. In the café, it's a house rule: always take the till key before the safe key.

The lab's explorer, a small program that tries every possible order of the two transfers' steps, counts it. The two naive transfers can interleave in 6 ways, and 2 of them deadlock. Ordered, there are 2 ways, and neither does. Reach for this fix first. Its price is discipline: every piece of code that takes two of these locks has to follow the order.

Remove no preemption with a timeout. (Preemption means taking something away from the one who holds it.) Lock the first account, then try the second with tryLock(10, MILLISECONDS), which gives up after 10 ms. If that fails, release the first, wait a random moment and start again. The thread takes the lock away from itself. The random wait matters. Without it, both threads can retry in step forever, each getting its first lock and failing on its second. It's like two people in a corridor who keep stepping aside the same way. That's a livelock: as busy as a deadlock is idle, and just as stuck.

Remove hold and wait by taking every lock at once, inside one big lock that guards the taking. It's simple and correct, and it lets only one transfer take its locks at a time, across the whole program.

Remove mutual exclusion by not locking at all. A single counter can be an AtomicLong, a Java number that changes through CAS. A transfer can't, because two balances must change together, and CAS works on one word.

One order for every lock leaves no room for a loop. Sort before you lock.

Databases meet the same problem when two transactions (groups of changes that must happen together or not at all) lock the same rows. They detect deadlocks instead of preventing them. PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, waits on a lock for deadlock_timeout, 1 s by default, and then builds a wait-for graph. If it finds a loop, it cancels one transaction with a deadlock error. The JVM only reports. In the lab you build that report yourself: the wait-for graph from a real jstack dump, the loop in it, and the proof that ordering removes it.

Every lock in this lesson guards data in memory that threads share. Next, we'll ask what that memory really is, and how two programs can use the same address without ever meeting.

try.title: Run the two fixes
steps: ordered locks the smaller account number first in both transfers. trylock uses a ReentrantLock for each account and tryLock(10 ms) on the second one, waiting a random 1 to 99 ms when it fails.
Predict which one prints a retry.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l05/demo/Transfers.java java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers ordered java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers trylock

try.expect:
pid 40: ordered locks
merchant 9960, customer 540
pid 63: trylock locks
refund done after 1 attempt(s)
payment done after 2 attempt(s)
merchant 9960, customer 540

Both finish with the right balances. The ordered version never retries: the second transfer waits for ACC-1001 while holding nothing. In the trylock version, both transfers grab their first lock, one times out on its second, lets go and retries after its random pause. Which one retries changes from run to run.

aside.title: Would a fair lock prevent the deadlock?
aside.html: No. A fair lock (new ReentrantLock(true) in Java) hands a freed lock to the thread that has waited longest, instead of whichever thread grabs it first. In a deadlock, no lock is ever freed, so there's nothing to hand over. Fairness changes who goes next, never whether anyone can go. It also costs speed, because every hand-over wakes a sleeping thread through the kernel, instead of letting a running thread take the lock.

opening:
Picture a customer at the café who sends back a cold coffee and buys a fresh one. At the same instant, the payments program starts two jobs: a refund from the shop's balance to the customer's, and a payment from the customer's balance back to the shop's. Then nothing happens. The card reader waits. The program uses no CPU at all, writes no error, and never answers again.

It's easy to think a stuck program must be busy, looping somewhere, and to go looking for the busy spot. Slow programs usually look like that. This one is asleep, and it's waiting for itself.

In CPU scheduling: EEVDF, nice and CPU quotas, the scheduler handed out turns without asking what a thread was doing. Now two threads need the same data at once. In this lesson, we'll build a lock from one machine instruction, see how Linux keeps the kernel, the core of the operating system, out of it until a thread must wait, and then cause a deadlock on purpose and fix it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a refund and a payment that froze the payments program at zero CPU. Each held one account's lock and waited for the other's, and the kernel saw only two sleeping threads. Locking the smaller account number first made the loop impossible.

If you write code with locks, search it for places that take two locks at once, and check that every one of them takes them in the same order. And if a Java program ever hangs at zero CPU, run jstack on it before you restart it.

Next, we'll look at the memory those threads share, and find out how two programs can use the same address without ever meeting.

compare.title: The transfer before and after lock ordering

a.label: naive: source, then target
a.title: deadlocks when two transfers cross
a.html: void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) { synchronized (from) { synchronized (to) { from.balance -= amount; to.balance += amount; } } }

b.label: ordered: smaller id first
b.title: cannot deadlock
b.html: void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) { Account first = from.id.compareTo(to.id) < 0 ? from : to; Account second = first == from ? to : from; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.balance -= amount; to.balance += amount; } } }

compare.note: The body is the same, and so are the locks. Only the order changes: from the part an account plays in this call (source or target) to something that belongs to the account itself, its id. Two transfers between the same accounts now ask for the locks in the same order, so one of them always waits before it holds anything. The order needs a key that two accounts never share. Account ids work. System.identityHashCode, a number Java gives each object, doesn't, because two objects can get the same one.

worked.title: Find and fix a deadlock in a running JVM

steps.say: The symptom: payments hang, and the program uses almost no CPU. Start from the kernel's side. Threads at 0% CPU, asleep in futex_wait_queue, are waiting for a lock or for a signal from another thread. That alone doesn't prove a deadlock, because idle threads waiting for work look the same.
steps.code: ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,stat,wchan:20,comm | grep -E "TID|refund|payment" # TID %CPU STAT WCHAN COMMAND # 62 0.0 Sl futex_wait_queue refund # 63 0.0 Sl futex_wait_queue payment

steps.say: Ask the JVM for the loop. jstack runs the same wait-for-graph search the lab builds. Add -l so it also lists who owns each ReentrantLock (it calls them "Locked ownable synchronizers").
steps.code: jstack -l $pid | sed -n '/Found one Java-level deadlock/,/^Java stack/p' # "refund": # waiting to lock monitor ... (object 0x000000008bb18d78, a sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers$Account), # which is held by "payment" # "payment": # waiting to lock monitor ... (object 0x000000008bb18d30, a sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers$Account), # which is held by "refund"

steps.say: Read the two stacks below the summary. A stack lists the methods a thread is in the middle of, the innermost first. Both threads sit on the same line of the same method, each holding one Account and waiting for the other. Same code, arguments in opposite order: the lock order comes from the call, not from the data.
steps.code:
"refund":
	at sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers.transfer(Transfers.java:21)
	- waiting to lock <0x000000008bb18d78> (a sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers$Account)
	- locked <0x000000008bb18d30> (a sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers$Account)

steps.say: Fix it by ordering on the account id, which removes circular wait, and restart the program, because nothing frees the stuck threads. Then prove the fix under the same timing.
steps.code: Account first = from.id.compareTo(to.id) < 0 ? from : to; // ACC-1001 before ACC-2002, always Account second = first == from ? to : from; // java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l05.demo.Transfers ordered // merchant 9960, customer 540

lab.title: Find the loop in a real deadlock dump
steps: Open the two dumps. Both are jstack -l output from the lab box: this lesson's Transfers naive (with synchronized), and the same deadlock built with two ReentrantLocks. In each thread's section, find the - locked, - waiting to lock, - parking to wait for and "Locked ownable synchronizers" lines.
Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All nine fail for now.

Write LockDump.parse. For each line that matches HEADER, a pattern for the first line of a thread's section, take the lines after it while they're blank or start with a space or a tab. The locks a thread holds come from LOCKED and OWNABLE matches, and the lock it waits for from the first WAITING match.
Write WaitForGraph.edges: map every held lock's address to the thread that holds it, then each waiting thread to the holder of the lock it wants.
Write findCycle. Each thread waits for at most one other, so following the arrows from a thread either ends or comes back to a thread already on your path.
Write Fix.breaks and Schedules.orderedTransfer. The last two tests use the explorer that's written for you: 2 deadlocks in 6 orders for the naive transfers, none once they're ordered.
hints: The main thread shows - waiting on <0x...> and - locked <0x...> for the same object. That's Object.wait(), which has given the lock back while it waits for a signal, so WAITING deliberately doesn't match it.

The deadlock summary at the end of a dump repeats "refund": without nid=, so HEADER skips it. Stop a thread's section at the first line that starts with a character other than a space, or the summary's lock lines end up in the last thread's section.

In findCycle, once you meet a thread that's already on the path, the loop is the path from that thread's first position to the end. Rotate it so the smallest name comes first: cycle.drop(i) + cycle.take(i).

drill.title: Order the locks, name the conditions
drill.prompt: From memory, write a Kotlin transfer(from, to, amount) that can't deadlock with synchronized. Then list the four conditions for a deadlock and, for each one, a fix that removes it.

answer.html: fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, amount: Long) { val (first, second) = if (from.id < to.id) from to to else to to from // one global order: by id synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { from.balance -= amount to.balance += amount } } } // mutual exclusion -> no lock at all: CAS on one word (AtomicLong), only for single-word updates // hold and wait -> take every lock at once, under one global lock // no preemption -> tryLock(timeout) the second, release the first, random back-off, retry // circular wait -> lock in a global order (above)

recap: A lock is built on compare-and-swap: one instruction that reads, compares and writes a word with no other CPU in between. A flag you check and then set is not a lock.

A futex is a 32-bit word in the program's own memory plus a wait queue in the kernel. Taking and releasing the lock are atomic instructions; the futex() system call is made only to sleep (FUTEX_WAIT) or to wake someone (FUTEX_WAKE).
FUTEX_WAIT sleeps only if the word still holds the expected value, and otherwise fails with EAGAIN. That check prevents lost wake-ups, and it's the errors column in strace -c.

A deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. A loop in the wait-for graph is the deadlock: jstack finds it, while the kernel only sees threads asleep in futex_wait_queue.
Remove any one condition: a lock order (circular wait), tryLock with a random wait (no preemption), all locks at once (hold and wait), or CAS instead of a lock (mutual exclusion).
The limit: a lock is only free while nobody else wants it. Under contention, every wait costs system calls and wake-ups, and the cure is less sharing, not a faster lock.

explain.prompt: A friend tests the payments program with one pretend card reader, and its synchronized blocks cost nothing. With 50 readers, 30% of the CPU goes to sys time, time spent in the kernel. They ask what changed inside the lock. Explain it to them.
explain.answer: The lock is a number in memory. When nobody else holds it, taking it is one compare-and-swap and releasing it is one atomic swap, a few nanoseconds each, and the kernel never hears about it. That's the one-reader case. With 50 readers, threads often find the lock already taken. Spinning would waste their turns on the CPU, so the JVM puts them to sleep, and on Linux that's a futex(FUTEX_WAIT) system call: the kernel puts the thread on a wait queue for that address. Every release that finds waiters makes a FUTEX_WAKE call, and each woken thread has to be scheduled again, often only to find the lock taken by someone else. Those system calls, sleeps, wake-ups and context switches are the sys time. The cure isn't a faster lock. It's less contention: hold the lock for less time, keep slow work like calls to the bank outside it, or split the shared data so threads don't all need the same lock.

deeper.html:
A ReentrantLock deadlock looks different in a dump, which is why the lab parses two files. The waiting thread is WAITING (parking). The lock is an object of the class all of Java's locks are built on (AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, or AQS), and its owner shows only under jstack -l:

"refund" #25 [58] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.53ms elapsed=3.15s tid=0x0000ffff7c1498d0 nid=58 waiting on condition  [...]
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@25.0.5/Native Method)
	- parking to wait for  <0x000000008bb17020> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)
	...
   Locked ownable synchronizers:
	- <0x000000008bb16ff0> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)

The summary at the end says "waiting for ownable synchronizer" instead of "waiting to lock monitor". Without -l, you see what each thread waits for, but not who owns it.

Why the default lock isn't fair. NonfairSync is the default. A non-fair lock lets a running thread take a lock that was just released, ahead of threads that are asleep, because waking a sleeping thread takes a system call and a trip through the scheduler, while the running thread is already on a CPU. new ReentrantLock(true) hands the lock to the longest waiter instead, and pays for it in speed.

Not every futex_wait_queue is a lock. Object.wait(), Condition.await(), CountDownLatch.await() and an idle thread pool's take() all sleep through the same futex call. In a dump, - waiting on <0x...> and parking to wait for a ConditionObject or CountDownLatch$Sync are waits for a signal from another thread, not for a lock, and no thread "holds" them. That's why the lab's graph only draws an arrow when some thread really holds the address.

Databases detect where the JVM only reports. PostgreSQL's documentation explains the 1 s default of deadlock_timeout plainly: the check is "relatively expensive", so the server assumes deadlocks are rare and only looks for a loop once a lock wait has lasted that long. Oracle, another database program, reports ORA-00060 in one of the sessions in the loop. Either way, your code must catch the error and run the transaction again, which is one more reason to lock rows in a fixed order in the first place.
